questions.question_text: Which reciprocal trigonometric function has fundamental period $180^\circ$, vertical asymptotes at $x = 180^\circ k$ for integers $k$, and $x$-intercepts at $x = 90^\circ + 180^\circ k$?

options.why: tan x has vertical asymptotes at 90 degrees + 180k degrees, not at multiples of 180 degrees.
sec x has period 360 degrees and has no x-intercepts.
cosec x has period 360 degrees and has no x-intercepts.

questions.solution_text:
$y = \cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ has period $180^\circ$.
It has vertical asymptotes where $\sin x = 0$ (at $x = 180^\circ k$) and $x$-intercepts where $\cos x = 0$ (at $x = 90^\circ + 180^\circ k$).

questions.question_text: What are the equations of all vertical asymptotes of $y = \sec x$ on the degree interval $[-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$?

options.why: These are the vertical asymptotes of cosecant and cotangent where sin x = 0.
Omitted the negative vertical asymptote at x = -90 degrees in the domain.
Used 45 degrees where cos x = 1/sqrt(2) instead of the zeros of cosine.

questions.solution_text:
Vertical asymptotes of $y = \sec x$ occur where $\cos x = 0$.
On $[-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$, $\cos x = 0$ at $x = -90^\circ$ and $x = 90^\circ$.

questions.question_text: What is the range of the function $y = 5\operatorname{cosec} x$ across its natural domain?

options.why: Stated the range of 5*sin x instead of its reciprocal 5*cosec x.
Omitted the negative branch where cosec x is less than or equal to -1.
Forgot to scale the range by the vertical dilation factor 5.

questions.solution_text:
The range of $\operatorname{cosec} x$ is $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.
Multiplying by $5$ scales the range to $(-\infty, -5] \cup [5, \infty)$.

questions.question_text: State the fundamental period (in degrees) of the reciprocal trigonometric function $y = \cot\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$.

options.why: Divided the period by 3 instead of multiplying by the reciprocal factor 3.
Used the 360 degree period of sine/cosine instead of the 180 degree period of cotangent.
Ignored the horizontal dilation factor 1/3 inside the argument.

questions.solution_text:
The base period of $\cot x$ is $180^\circ$.
For $\cot(nx)$ with $n = \dfrac{1}{3}$, the period is $\dfrac{180^\circ}{1/3} = 180^\circ \times 3 = 540^\circ$.

questions.question_text: Where do the $x$-intercepts of $y = \cot x$ lie in the interval $[0, 4\pi]$?

options.why: These are the vertical asymptotes of cot x on [0, 4*pi] where sin x = 0.
Listed intercepts on [0, 2*pi] only, omitting the second half of the [0, 4*pi] interval.
These are points where cot x = 1 or -1 rather than zeros.

questions.solution_text:
$\cot x = 0 \iff \cos x = 0$.
In $[0, 4\pi]$, the zeros of cosine are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{2}, \dfrac{7\pi}{2}$.

questions.question_text: Find all solutions to the equation $\operatorname{cosec} x = -\sqrt{2}$ in the domain $[0, 360^\circ]$.

options.why: Selected the Quadrant 1 and Quadrant 2 angles where cosecant is positive.
Used a reference angle of 30 degrees instead of 45 degrees.
Used a reference angle of 60 degrees instead of 45 degrees.

questions.solution_text:
$\operatorname{cosec} x = -\sqrt{2} \implies \sin x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
Sine is negative in Quadrants $3$ and $4$ with base angle $45^\circ$:
$x = 180^\circ + 45^\circ = 225^\circ$
$x = 360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ$.

questions.question_text: How many solutions does the equation $\cot x = 7$ have in the domain $[0, 6\pi]$?

options.why: Assumed cotangent has period 2*pi and counted 3 periods on [0, 6*pi].
Doubled the count by assuming two intersections per period.
Assumed 7 exceeds the range of cotangent.

questions.solution_text:
The interval $[0, 6\pi]$ spans a length of $6\pi$.
Because the period of $\cot x$ is $\pi$, the interval contains exactly $6$ periods (branches).
Since $\cot x$ decreases strictly from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$ on each branch $(k\pi, (k+1)\pi)$, it equals $7$ exactly once per branch.
Total number of solutions $= 6$.

questions.question_text: What are the coordinates of the local minimum of $y = 4\sec x + 3$ in the interval $[-\pi, \pi]$?

options.why: Found the local maximum on the negative branch at x = pi instead of the local minimum.
Forgot to add the vertical shift +3 to the amplitude.
Placed the minimum at the asymptote x = pi/2 where sec x is undefined.

questions.solution_text:
On $[-\pi, \pi]$, the positive branch of $\sec x$ has its local minimum at $x = 0$, where $\sec(0) = 1$.
Substituting $x = 0$ gives $y = 4(1) + 3 = 7$.
Local minimum is $(0, 7)$.

questions.question_text: Which pair of functions do not have the same domain as each other?

options.why: Both exclude integer multiples of pi from their domains.
Both are defined for every real input.
Both inverse functions have the same domain interval [-1,1].

questions.solution_text: $\sec x$ is undefined when $\cos x=0$, while $\cosec x$ is undefined when $\sin x=0$. These excluded input sets differ, so option C is the pair with different domains.
